```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(muscal)
```

DISTATIS combines several distance matrices on the same objects. For a sorting
task, each assessor groups products by perceived similarity. The analysis gives
an object map representing the panel's consensus, a separate assessor map showing
agreement between sorts, and partial object maps showing each assessor's view.
Use `covstatis()` when your inputs are covariance or connectivity matrices;
use `distatis()` when they are distances.

## Sorting the beers

Abdi, Valentin, Chollet, and Chrea (2007) report eight beers sorted by ten
assessors. The following is Table 1 of their paper. Numbers identify groups within
each assessor's column; the group labels themselves carry no numeric meaning.

```{r beer-data}
partitions <- matrix(c(
  1,4,3,4,1,1,2,2,1,3,
  4,5,2,5,2,3,1,1,4,3,
  3,1,2,3,2,4,3,1,1,2,
  4,2,3,3,1,1,1,2,1,4,
  1,5,3,5,2,1,1,2,1,3,
  2,3,1,1,3,5,4,4,3,1,
  1,4,3,4,1,1,2,2,2,4,
  5,2,4,2,4,2,5,3,4,5
), 8, 10, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(
  c("Affligen", "Budweiser", "Buckler Blonde", "Killian", "St. Landelin",
    "Buckler Highland", "Fruit Defendu", "EKU28"), paste0("A", 1:10)))

distances <- sorting_distances(partitions)
fit <- distatis(distances, ncomp = 4)
fit
round(fit$alpha, 3)
```

`sorting_distances()` assigns zero to a pair placed in the same group, and one
to a pair placed in different groups. It accepts matrices or data frames,
including columns with character labels or factors. An all-in-one-group sort has
no contrast and is rejected during fitting because its RV similarities are undefined.

## Object and assessor maps

```{r objects, fig.cap="Consensus map of the eight beers."}
ggplot2::autoplot(fit, type = "objects", labels = TRUE)
```

The default normalization divides each assessor's centered Gram matrix by its
largest eigenvalue. DISTATIS then computes RV similarities between those tables,
uses the leading RV eigenvector to obtain nonnegative weights summing to one,
and eigendecomposes the weighted compromise. High assessor weight means agreement
with this panel; it is not an external measure of accuracy.

```{r assessors, fig.cap="Assessor principal coordinates in RV space."}
ggplot2::autoplot(fit, type = "subjects", labels = TRUE)
```

Object and assessor maps have different spectra. Their axes need not have the
same rank or interpretation. Requesting `ncomp = 4` retains at most four positive
axes in each map. Axis percentages always use the full inertia, rather than
renormalizing the retained axes to 100%.

```{r spectra}
round(fit$eigenvalues, 3)
round(fit$interstructure_eigenvalues, 3)
fit$compromise_quality
sum(fit$inertia[1:4])
```

These reproduce the paper's eigenvalues and approximately 60% agreement summary.
The first four object axes account for 82.285% of the computed inertia. The
supplied author manuscript's prose gives 84%; that figure does not agree with
its eigenvalues, so the package reports the computed ratio.

```{r partials, fig.cap="Partial maps for three assessors, connected to the compromise."}
plot_partial_scores(fit, blocks = 1:3)
```

Each partial map contains one point per object. The compromise is their weighted
mean, using `fit$alpha`. These maps describe variation across assessors; their
spread is not a confidence region.

```{r barycenter}
weighted_partial <- Reduce(`+`, Map(`*`, fit$partial_scores, fit$alpha))
max(abs(weighted_partial - multivarious::scores(fit)))
```

`plot_block_weights(fit)` and `plot_block_similarity(fit)` display the weights
and RV matrix. `plot_variance(fit)` shows the complete object spectrum;
`plot_variance(fit, axes = "subjects")` shows the assessor spectrum.

## General distances and squared distances

`distatis()` accepts a list of `dist` objects or square numeric matrices, a
three-dimensional object-by-object-by-assessor array, or a single distance table.
Objects must have the same order and, when supplied, consistent names in every
table. Unnamed inputs are aligned by position.

```{r general-distances}
coordinates <- cbind(c(0, 1, 3, 5), c(0, 2, 1, 4))
D <- as.matrix(dist(coordinates))
ordinary <- distatis(D, norm_method = "none", ncomp = 3)
already_squared <- distatis(D^2, squared = TRUE, norm_method = "none", ncomp = 3)
max(abs(ordinary$compromise_full - already_squared$compromise_full))
```

The default is ordinary distances, as produced by R's `dist()`. Set
`squared = TRUE` only when the entries are already squared. Binary sorting
distances cannot reveal a mistaken squaring convention, so check this setting
when using other distances. `norm_method = "frobenius"` and `"none"` are also
available; RV similarities determine weights under all normalization choices.

Non-Euclidean distances with materially negative Gram eigenvalues are rejected,
with the assessor name and negative inertia in the error. No correction is
silently applied. The `tol` argument controls relative numerical tolerances.

## Supplementary assessors and reconstruction

Project a new assessor's distances on the fitted objects using
`project_distance()`. For both the assessor coordinates and object partial maps,
use `project_subjects()`. Neither function changes the fitted compromise.

```{r supplementary}
partial <- project_distance(fit, distances[[1]])
max(abs(partial - fit$partial_scores[[1]]))
supplementary <- project_subjects(fit, distances[1:2])
supplementary$scalar_summaries
max(abs(supplementary$subject_scores - fit$subject_scores[1:2, ]))
```

Supplementary distances use the fit's `squared` setting unless overridden.
The RV summary compares with the full compromise. `distance_to_compromise` is
the Frobenius distance to that full normalized matrix;
`distance_to_subspace` is the residual from the retained object subspace.
These are different diagnostics. Projecting new objects would require a separate
out-of-sample MDS procedure and is not supported here.

```{r reconstruction}
gram <- multivarious::reconstruct(fit)
compromise_distances <- multivarious::reconstruct(fit, what = "distance")
dim(compromise_distances)
```

Reconstruction uses retained object components. Distances are in normalized
compromise units, rather than any original assessor's units. Use all positive
object components when full reconstruction is required.

`project_table_covariate()` and `project_feature_covariate()` project assessor
and object covariates into the corresponding maps. Their cosines and regression
slopes are uncentered; center covariates yourself if that matches your question.
The existing COVSTATIS inference adapters are explicitly unavailable for
DISTATIS: their raw-inner-product refits do not implement its RV geometry.

## Reference

Abdi, H., Valentin, D., Chollet, S., & Chrea, C. (2007). Analyzing assessors and
products in sorting tasks: DISTATIS, theory and applications. *Food Quality and
Preference*, 18, 627-640. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2006.09.003>.
